p160.002: On September 18, when they were given a week of rest, most of the apostles went home to see their families. But Nathaniel and Thomas were very busy. The reason was Rodan, a Greek philosopher from Alexandria. Rodan had recently become a disciple of Jesus, and he had come to Magadan hoping to weave together the philosophy he had studied and the teachings of Jesus. Jesus welcomed Rodan warmly but did not take part in the discussions himself; he told Nathaniel and Thomas to listen carefully to him and share the gospel with him. This paper sums up the talks Rodan gave.
p160.004: Rodan said that human life is moved by three forces: urges, desires, and lures that draw us toward something higher. A person of strong character is one who turns inborn urges into good social living and passing desires into higher, lasting dreams. Animals do not ask about the meaning of life, but human beings are able to see values and meanings. Rodan said that discouragement, worry, and laziness are signs of moral immaturity, and that a mature person looks on those who are less grown-up with a parent's patience.
p160.005: To solve a problem well, we must first honestly admit what the difficulty is. People often turn away from their problems out of fear or pride, but only those with courage look the truth straight in the face. And to win the cooperation of others, tact and tolerance are a must.
p160.006: Rodan said that the greatest way of solving problems he had learned from Jesus was the time of worship, withdrawing alone to commune with God. Jesus often prayed alone and gave his heart over to the Father, saying, “⟦Q 160:1.11⟧Not my will, but yours, be done.⟦/Q⟧” This kind of worship rests the mind, takes away fear, and gives courage. Rodan admitted that his own philosophy had lacked direction and power, and that Jesus' gospel filled in what was missing.
p160.008: Rodan said that what sets humans apart from animals is that they can share thoughts and ideals through words and symbols. Because of this ability to share meanings, culture and civilization come into being. The best social group is the family, and true friendship also helps a person grow a great deal.
p160.009: Friendship and love bring four gifts. First, we can open our hearts to one another and be understood. Second, by pooling our wisdom we can avoid prejudice and narrow thinking. This is why Jesus always sent his disciples out two by two. Third, friends renew our zest and courage for living and add to our joy. Fourth, when we share hardships and sorrows, the pain becomes much smaller. Rodan said these relationships come about most beautifully in a marriage and a home where people truly care for each other.
p160.011: Then where does the power we need to grow mature come from? Rodan said that emotional excitement actually drains our strength. The secret is worship, which is communion with God. Worship, through quiet thinking in meditation and the rest of letting go, turns weakness into strength, fear into courage, and our own will into God's will. When it becomes a habit, it is hard at first, but later it actually becomes a rest and even saves time.
p160.012: Rodan said that there are times when we must fight for what is right, but Jesus wins the same victory more easily through tact and tolerance. He reported Jesus' saying that a “⟦Q 160:3.4⟧wise man, when seeking entrance through the locked door, would not destroy the door but rather would seek for the key wherewith to unlock it⟦/Q⟧”. A person who holds a high goal can be freed from small quarrels such as worry, jealousy, and revenge.
p160.014: Even while looking toward eternal goals, we must faithfully take care of our life now. Rodan named health, clear thinking, ability and skill, the wealth needed for living, the strength to bear defeat, and education and wisdom as things life truly needs. He said that skill gives great satisfaction in life, so we should learn to do at least one thing well, and not be fooled by the sweet rewards of dishonest ways. He also told them to keep good memories, especially the precious moments of friendship, like a gallery in the mind.
p160.015: Above all, we must learn to accept failure gracefully. If we hide failure behind a forced smile, we end up facing even greater disappointment. Success gives courage, but wisdom comes when we accept failure and learn from it. For someone who seeks God, failure is not the end; it is only one step in learning wisdom.
p160.017: Rodan said that religion is a wholehearted response to the highest ideal that all people can honor. Religion is not just an idea believed in the head; it is action shown in one's life. And true religion seeks to change people and to change the world. Rodan said that without the supreme ideal of the eternal God, there can be no true spiritual religion.
p160.018: Rodan said that Jesus' religion is the highest religious idea in the world. That is because Jesus did not speak of God only as a faraway ideal; he taught that God is a loving Father whom anyone can actually meet by entering the kingdom of heaven. Rodan declared, “⟦Q 160:5.8⟧I am a believer, I have embarked⟦/Q⟧”, and said he would set out on this eternal adventure.
p160.019: True religion does not come from feeling or thinking that we want to be like God; it needs a living spiritual experience. Rodan's talks show the way of growing mature through friends and family, through failure and worship. If we too are good friends, are honest when we fail, and take quiet time to talk with God, we can grow more mature step by step.
p161.002: On September 25, Jesus surprised everyone by announcing that the next morning he would go with the twelve apostles to Jerusalem for the Feast of Tabernacles. But Nathaniel and Thomas were still in the middle of their discussions with Rodan, the Greek philosopher, so with Jesus' permission they stayed at Magadan a few more days. They also learned that in Alexandria Rodan had been well taught in Jesus' teachings by a former disciple of John the Baptist. During the past week Rodan had talked about his philosophy; this time Thomas and Nathaniel took turns sharing the gospel of the kingdom with Rodan, and they discussed things deeply together.
p161.004: The question on which Rodan and the two apostles disagreed was whether God is a personality. Put simply, a personality means a personal being who can know others and share hearts with them. Rodan argued that to be a personality, one must be able to communicate fully with an equal, and since God is infinite and has no equal, he must be beyond personality. When the two apostles asked Jesus for help, Jesus did not join the discussion; he only told Thomas that if he knew the Father spiritually, it did not matter very much what idea of him he held.
p161.005: In the end Thomas gave up the argument, but Nathaniel won Rodan over. Nathaniel first pointed out that the Father communicates fully with the Eternal Son and the Infinite Spirit, who are his equals. He also said that the very way Jesus, the Son of God, lived sharing his heart with people was proof that God and man can communicate with each other. And he said that God must be a personality, because he is the one who made all personalities and the destination that all personalities will at last reach.
p161.006: Rodan finally said he would confess God as a personality. But he added a condition: God must be infinitely greater than what people think of as personality. Rodan said that “⟦Q 161:1.11⟧while God must be infinitely more than a personality, he cannot be anything less⟦/Q⟧”, and he accepted Jesus as the one who shows us the Father.
p161.008: The question that remained was the teaching that Jesus is divine. Nathaniel and Thomas told why they believed it. Jesus was the most unselfish friend in the world; he was the friend of sinners, and he loved even his enemies. He scolded the apostles at times, but anyone could see that he truly loved them. The more you knew him, the more you loved him.
p161.009: The apostles believed that Jesus was always without sin. Jesus prayed for the apostles, but he never asked them to pray for him, and he never did anything he needed to repent of. The apostles' devotion came from repentance, but Jesus' devotion came from righteousness. Jesus was always moved when he saw people suffering; he was fair and yet merciful, kind and yet brave.
p161.010: Jesus also knew about things that happened where he was not present, and he seemed to know the thoughts in people's hearts. When he asked questions, it was not to get information but to draw out what the other person was really thinking. Jesus said astonishing things like “⟦Q 161:2.9⟧Before Abraham was, I am.⟦/Q⟧” and said “⟦Q 161:2.9⟧that anyone who has seen him has seen the Father⟦/Q⟧”, and he said them as naturally as a child. The two apostles said they were convinced that Jesus was both the Son of Man and the Son of God.
p161.011: When the discussions were over, Nathaniel and Thomas hurried to Jerusalem to join the other apostles. Rodan went back to Alexandria and taught philosophy for many years. He lived as a faithful believer all his life and gave his life in Greece during a time of persecution.
p161.013: The Urantia Book explains how Jesus' human mind and divine mind worked together. Jesus' awareness that he was God grew little by little until his baptism. After that, it seems, Jesus could choose for himself whether to use only his human mind or also the knowledge of his divine mind. Sometimes he knew and acted only as much as an ordinary person would; at other times he acted with wisdom beyond human ability.
p161.014: Jesus often hid his knowledge of the future and of people's hearts, so that his disciples would not feel that all their thoughts were being read. The Urantia Book honestly says that how these two minds were joined and worked as one is a mystery we cannot fully understand. Like Rodan and the apostles, who kept talking all the way through hard questions until they found the truth, we too can honestly ask about what we wonder and think it through together.
p162.002: Jesus and the ten apostles planned to travel to Jerusalem by the shorter road through Samaria. At sunset Philip and Matthew went into a village to find a place to stay, but the villagers, who strongly disliked Jews, drove them away with sticks and stones. Angry, James and John asked Jesus to call down fire from heaven to destroy the village. Jesus sternly rebuked them: “⟦Q 162:0.2⟧Vengeance savors not of the outlook of the kingdom of heaven.⟦/Q⟧” Then they went on to another village. The group arrived at Bethany, and for about the next six weeks Jesus stayed near Jerusalem and in Bethlehem.
p162.003: 1. The Dangers of the Visit to Jerusalem
p162.004: In the past, the disciples had begged Jesus to go to Jerusalem and teach there. But now they knew that the Sanhedrin, the highest Jewish council, wanted to kill him, and they were all afraid. Until then Jesus had always said, “⟦Q 162:1.1⟧The hour has not yet come⟦/Q⟧”, but this time he said, “⟦Q 162:1.1⟧But the hour has come⟦/Q⟧”. When Jesus boldly taught in the temple, the rumor that he was running away in fear completely disappeared.
p162.005: His enemies could not easily seize him. There were secret believers in Jesus even inside the Sanhedrin, and many of the people gathered for the feast were friendly toward him. His enemies also saw how bold he was and guessed that the Roman authorities might have promised to protect him. People's opinions were divided—some called him a good man, others a prophet, the Messiah, or a troublemaker—but even his enemies were amazed at the teaching of a man who had never studied under the rabbis.
p162.007: On the first day Jesus taught in the temple, someone asked how he could teach like that when he had never studied with the rabbis. Jesus answered that this teaching was not his own but belonged to the One who sent him, and that anyone who wanted to do the Father's will would know whether it came from God. He also said that the leaders wanted to kill him because he was teaching a gospel that set people free from heavy traditions.
p162.008: The Sanhedrin sent an officer named Eber to arrest Jesus. Jesus told him not to be afraid but to come close and listen, and he said that he held no ill will toward anyone. After hearing Jesus, Eber went back without arresting him and reported, “⟦Q 162:2.9⟧we never heard a man speak like this man⟦/Q⟧”. Then he asked the leaders whether they could condemn a man without even hearing him.
p162.010: On the morning of the third day of the feast, men hired by the Sanhedrin dragged in a woman who had been caught doing wrong and asked Jesus whether she should be stoned as the law said. It was a trap: whatever Jesus answered, they meant to use it against him. The Urantia Book explains that this woman was being forced and used by a wicked husband, and that the husband had plotted this with Jesus' enemies.
p162.011: Jesus walked over near the husband, who was hiding behind the crowd, and wrote a few words in the sand, and the husband hurried away. Then he wrote on the ground again in front of the woman's accusers, and they too left one by one. When only the woman was left, Jesus said, “⟦Q 162:3.5⟧neither do I condemn you. Go your way in peace.⟦/Q⟧” This woman, Hildana, left her wicked husband and became a disciple of the kingdom.
p162.013: The feast of tabernacles was a festival of thanks for the autumn harvest, and Jews came to it from all over the world, from Spain to India. People lived in booths covered with leaves, and at night they enjoyed the feast under the great candlesticks and torches that lit up the temple. The priests brought water from the pool of Siloam in a golden pitcher and poured it on the altar, a ceremony that stood for the pouring out of God's spirit. A feast that gathered so many people was the right time for Jesus to boldly proclaim his gospel before the whole world.
p162.014: 5. Sermon on the Light of the World
p162.015: On the evening before the last day of the feast, while the candlesticks and torches were shining brightly, Jesus stood up and said: “⟦Q 162:5.2⟧I am the light of the world. He who follows me shall not walk in darkness but shall have the light of life.⟦/Q⟧” Jesus said that he knew where he came from and where he was going, and that the Father was always with him. He also said that the Father loves even his children who go wrong. Many believed, and no one dared to lay a hand on Jesus.
p162.016: 6. Discourse on the Water of Life
p162.017: On the great day of the feast, just after the priests had poured the water and the wine on the altar, Jesus stood among the pilgrims and called out, “⟦Q 162:6.1⟧If any man thirst, let him come to me and drink.⟦/Q⟧” Jesus said that he had brought the water of life from the Father, and that when his work was finished, the Spirit of Truth would be poured out on all people. The water ceremony of the temple was a good symbol, but now it was time for the true spirit that the symbol pointed to.
p162.019: On the afternoon of the last day, Jesus taught again in the temple: “⟦Q 162:7.2⟧the truth shall make you free⟦/Q⟧”. His listeners said that they were Abraham's children and slaves to no one, but Jesus was speaking not of the freedom of the body but of the freedom of the soul. A person who sins becomes a slave of sin, but when the Son sets you free and makes you a son of God, you are truly free.
p162.020: Jesus said that whoever keeps his words in his heart will never taste death. Then the people shouted, asking whether he was greater than Abraham. When Jesus said, “⟦Q 162:7.6⟧before Abraham was, I am⟦/Q⟧”, some rushed off to pick up stones, but Jesus quickly slipped out of the temple and went to Martha, Mary, and Lazarus, who were waiting for him near Bethany.
p162.021: 8. The Visit with Martha and Mary
p162.022: While Jesus was staying at the home of Martha and Mary, Mary and Lazarus sat at his feet listening to his teaching, and Martha was very busy getting supper ready. Martha was the kind of person whose mind was easily troubled by little things. When Martha complained that her sister was not helping, Jesus called her, “⟦Q 162:8.3⟧Martha, Martha⟦/Q⟧”, and asked why she worried about so many things. He said that Mary had chosen what was truly needed, but he also told the two of them to learn to work together and to refresh their souls together. There is a time for everything, and the smaller things must give way before the greater ones.
p162.024: After the feast Jesus did not teach in the temple again. Instead he spent his time going back and forth between Bethany and Bethlehem, and in Bethlehem he taught Abner, a former apostle of John the Baptist, and his companions. Moved by Jesus' courage and warm understanding, they all accepted the kingdom with their whole hearts and decided to join Jesus and the twelve apostles and work together with them from early November.
p162.025: At the end of October, Jesus and the apostles left Jerusalem and returned to the Magadan park. The apostles were greatly relieved, and they never again urged him to go to Jerusalem. Jesus boldly spoke the truth even in the face of danger, and he held no ill will even toward those who wanted to harm him. His example shows us what true courage is.
p163.002: A few days after Jesus and the apostles returned to Magadan, Abner came from Bethlehem with about fifty of his disciples. Gathered at the Magadan camp were the evangelistic corps, the women's corps, and about one hundred and fifty trusted disciples from all over Palestine. On November 4, Jesus began an intense course of training for them. Jesus gave a talk every morning; Peter taught them how to preach, Nathaniel how to teach, Thomas how to answer questions, and Matthew how to handle money.
p163.004: On the Sabbath afternoon of November 19, Jesus ordained seventy as messengers of the gospel and made Abner their leader. More than four hundred believers gathered by the lakeside to watch. Jesus said, “⟦Q 163:1.3⟧The harvest is indeed plenteous, but the laborers are few⟦/Q⟧”, and he told them he was sending them out like lambs among wolves. They were to go two by two, carrying no purse or extra clothing; they were to stay in a home that loved peace and not move from house to house because a better place was offered. And he urged them to “⟦Q 163:1.3⟧be as wise as serpents while you are also as harmless as doves⟦/Q⟧”.
p163.005: Jesus told them to announce everywhere they went that the kingdom of heaven was at hand, and to care for those who were sick in mind or body. Freely they had received, so freely they should give. Then he laid his hands, one by one, on the heads of the seventy as they knelt in a circle. The next day the thirty-five pairs set out for Galilee, Samaria, and Judea, and they taught for about six weeks.
p163.006: 2. The Rich Young Man and Others
p163.007: More than fifty of those who wanted to be among the seventy were not chosen. One said he would come after he had buried his father, and another said he would come after saying good-bye to his family. Jesus told them they could still remain faithful disciples, but that a gospel messenger had to lay everything down and could not have a divided heart. “⟦Q 163:2.3⟧No man, having put his hand to the plough, if he turns back⟦/Q⟧”, he said, could become a messenger of the kingdom.
p163.008: A rich young man named Matadormus, a member of the Sanhedrin, also came to Jesus. He said he had kept all the commandments since his youth and asked what more he should do. Jesus told him that salvation is the reward not of works but of faith, and that he was already a child of the kingdom. But when he said he wanted to be one of the seventy, Jesus kissed him on the forehead and told him to sell all his goods, give to the poor, and come follow him. Because he had great wealth, he went away sad.
p163.009: What Jesus wanted was to rescue him not from his wealth itself but from his love of wealth. The Urantia Book explains that almost everyone has some one thing they hold dear, and that to enter the kingdom they must let it go. Only some years later did Matadormus do as Jesus had said. Jesus did not say that owning wealth was wrong in itself, but again and again he rebuked the strong for unfairly taking advantage of the weak.
p163.011: After the young man had left, Jesus said that it is very hard for those who trust in riches to enter the kingdom of God. Amazed, Peter asked who then could be saved, and Jesus said that with God all things are possible. He also said that not every disciple has to give up his property, but that whatever stands between God and us must be laid down.
p163.012: When Peter asked what they, who had left everything, would receive, Jesus said they would receive many times over in this world and eternal life in the world to come. Then he told a story about a vineyard. The owner called workers many times, from morning until evening, and when the day was over, he gave those who came late one denarius, the same as those who had worked since morning. When the early workers complained, the owner answered that he had paid them what he had promised—were they jealous because he was generous? It means that God treats each person with love, according to that person's needs.
p163.014: On the morning the seventy were to leave, Jesus stressed several things. The gospel was to be preached to both Jews and gentiles; when they cared for the sick, they were not to lead people to expect miracles; and they were to proclaim not worldly power but the spiritual brotherhood of the sons of God. They were also to teach that the whole duty of man is contained in one commandment: love God with all your heart, and love your neighbor as yourself. They were to teach this instead of the hundreds of rules the Pharisees had made.
p163.015: Then Peter urged the seventy to treasure consecrated devotion, courage, faith and trust, zeal, kindness and courtesy, and the care of the sick. The saying “⟦Q 163:1.3⟧Salute no man by the way⟦/Q⟧” meant that they should not waste time on the long and complicated greeting customs of that day; it did not mean they should not greet people kindly. Peter said that anyone who was afraid could withdraw, but no one did.
p163.017: Jesus and the apostles moved their last headquarters near Pella in Perea, the place where Jesus had been baptized. On December 6, a group of about three hundred packed up and set out. This was beside the very spring where John the Baptist had once camped. Pilgrims came from many parts of the Roman Empire and even from the far East, so David Zebedee cut back his messenger service and, with those men, set up a separate large camp for the pilgrims. Even before the seventy returned, nearly eight hundred visitors had already gathered.
p163.019: On December 30, the seventy came back to Pella two by two and eagerly told what they had experienced. Seeing people spread the good news without him, Jesus knew that the work of the kingdom would go on even after he left. When the seventy boasted that even devils had obeyed them, Jesus told them not to rejoice too much over such things but to rejoice that their names were written in heaven.
p163.020: Filled with joy, Jesus thanked the Father for revealing this gospel not to those who thought themselves wise but to people like little children. He said that the prophets of old had longed to see what they were now seeing and hearing. The next day he sternly warned the seventy to beware of spiritual pride. And he gave them this invitation: “⟦Q 163:6.7⟧Come to me all you who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.⟦/Q⟧”
p163.022: The Pella camp was busy preparing for the last mission, a three-month tour through all of Perea. Now people came from all over the world without Jesus having to travel far. The women's corps had grown to fifty, and they made ready to visit and care for the sick and suffering, with Perpetua, Peter's wife, leading this work.
p163.023: Unlike the Galilean days, when crowds rushed in to see miracles, the kingdom at this time was in a stage of growing spiritually deeper. Even so, many still did not understand that the kingdom of God is the spiritual brotherhood of those who have God as their Father. To look at what holds our hearts most tightly, and to keep our hearts undivided toward God—that is the teaching of this paper.
p164.002: While the new camp was being set up at Pella, Jesus quietly set out for Jerusalem, taking only Nathaniel and Thomas with him. He meant to attend the feast of dedication. The two apostles were afraid he would be seized by the Sanhedrin and gave every reason they could think of to stop him, but Jesus answered only, “⟦Q 164:0.1⟧I would give these teachers in Israel another opportunity to see the light, before my hour comes.⟦/Q⟧” They spent the night at Jericho.
p164.004: That evening a lawyer, hoping to put Jesus in a difficult spot, asked him what he must do to gain eternal life. When Jesus asked him what was written in the law, he answered that it was to love God with all your heart and to love your neighbor as yourself. Then he asked again, “⟦Q 164:1.2⟧who is my neighbor?⟦/Q⟧” In those days the Jewish law counted only one's own people as neighbors, so this was a trap: if Jesus said anything different, they could accuse him of attacking the law.
p164.005: Jesus answered with a story. A man going down to Jericho fell among robbers and was left on the road half dead. A priest and a Levite saw him but passed by on the other side of the road. But a Samaritan, one of the people the Jews looked down on, felt compassion for him, bound up his wounds, took him to an inn, and even paid to have him cared for. When Jesus asked which of the three had turned out to be the neighbor, the lawyer, who did not even want to say the word 'Samaritan,' answered, “⟦Q 164:1.3⟧He who showed mercy on him.⟦/Q⟧” Jesus said, “⟦Q 164:1.3⟧Go and do likewise.⟦/Q⟧” Ever since, this story has encouraged brotherly love among believers.
p164.007: The only purpose of this visit was to give the Jewish leaders one last chance. On Friday night, about twenty-five Jewish leaders who believed Jesus' teaching gathered at the home of Nicodemus, and fourteen of them were members or former members of the Sanhedrin. They were all amazed at the deep wisdom Jesus showed, and they came to love him. They offered to stand with Jesus before the Sanhedrin, but Jesus stopped them, saying that it would only bring trouble on them. Instead, he said, he would make the kingdom known once more in the way the Father would show him.
p164.009: The next morning, a Sabbath, a beggar named Josiah, who had been blind from birth, was sitting near the temple. Nathaniel asked whose sin had caused this man to be blind. He asked because the rabbis of that time taught that being born blind was a punishment for sin. Jesus said that it was neither this man's sin nor his parents', but something that had happened in the natural course of events. Jesus always taught that we should not force spiritual causes onto ordinary bodily things.
p164.010: Jesus spat on the ground, made clay, put it on Josiah's eyes, and told him to go and wash in the pool of Siloam. When Josiah did so, he was able to see. He had not asked to be healed, and his faith was weak, but he did what Jesus said because people in those days believed that the spittle of a holy man had healing power. The Urantia Book explains that one reason Jesus used clay and water was to teach people not to look only for miracles when healing, but also to value the material ways of caring for the body.
p164.011: Jesus deliberately did this on the Sabbath, close to the temple. It was his way of openly challenging the Sanhedrin and the Pharisees and announcing his break with them.
p164.013: This caused a great stir, and the Sanhedrin even broke its own rule against meeting on the Sabbath to hold a session. But they were afraid to summon Jesus, so they called only Josiah. One Pharisee said that a man who does not keep the Sabbath is not from God, and a young member who secretly believed in Jesus answered back, asking how a sinner could do such a thing. Josiah answered that he thought Jesus was a prophet.
p164.014: The leaders called Josiah's parents, but the parents knew that anyone who believed in Jesus would be thrown out of the synagogue, so in fear they said only, ask our son himself. When the leaders pressed Josiah, saying that Jesus was a sinner, Josiah answered, “⟦Q 164:4.9⟧one thing I do know—that, whereas I was blind, now I see.⟦/Q⟧” When they kept on questioning him, he asked whether they too wanted to become his disciples.
p164.015: At last Josiah stood up on a bench and cried out that no one had ever heard of the eyes of a man born blind being opened, so if this man were not from God, he could not have done it. Angry, the leaders threw him out of the synagogue. At first Josiah had known little about Jesus; his brave testimony grew in his heart during the unfair trial.
p164.017: Meanwhile, Jesus was teaching the people close by in Solomon's Porch. When someone told him to say plainly whether he was the Messiah, Jesus said, “⟦Q 164:5.2⟧My sheep hear my voice and I know them and they follow me.⟦/Q⟧” And he said that no one could snatch them out of the Father's hand, and that the Father and he were one. Some tried to pick up stones, but Jesus slipped out of the temple.
p164.018: Jesus went to find Josiah, who had been thrown out of the synagogue, and asked him, “⟦Q 164:5.4⟧do you believe in the Son of God?⟦/Q⟧” When he heard that the one speaking to him was that very person, Josiah said, “⟦Q 164:5.4⟧Lord, I believe⟦/Q⟧”, and fell down in worship. Jesus took him to the Pella camp, and Josiah became a preacher of the gospel for the rest of his life. God warmly welcomed a simple man whom people had cast out. Josiah's courage in speaking the truth without fear is a good example for us too.
p165.002: On January 3, A.D. 30, Abner, the leader of the seventy messengers, gave his associates their final instructions and sent them out to the cities and villages of Perea. Perea was a beautiful region across the Jordan, where Jews and gentiles lived in about equal numbers. This Perean mission, which lasted almost three months, was Jesus' last ministry; after it he would go to Jerusalem to go through the final events of his life on earth.
p165.003: There were no miracles during this time, and the women's corps, which had grown to sixty-two, took on most of the care of the sick. No part of Palestine was reached by the gospel as thoroughly as Perea. Jesus sometimes stayed at the Pella camp, and sometimes went with the twelve apostles to visit and help in the cities where the seventy were working.
p165.005: By the middle of January more than twelve hundred people had gathered at Pella. When Jesus was at the camp, he usually taught the multitude at nine o'clock in the morning; Peter and the other apostles taught in the afternoon; and in the evening he held question-and-answer times with his close disciples. By the middle of March more than four thousand people were gathering every morning. Jesus decided to finish his work on earth when people's interest was at its highest, even without miracles. Most of those who gathered were seekers of truth, but there were also Pharisees among them, looking for something to criticize.
p165.007: More than three hundred Pharisees and teachers followed Jesus from Jerusalem all the way to Pella. In front of them and his disciples, Jesus told the story of the good shepherd. The true shepherd enters the sheepfold by the door, and the sheep know his voice and follow him. But the sheep will not follow the voice of a stranger. Jesus said that false shepherds neither feed the sheep well nor protect them.
p165.008: Then Jesus said that he was both the door to the sheepfold and the true shepherd. A hired worker runs away when the wolf comes, but the true shepherd lays down even his life for the sheep. Jesus said that there were many other sheep not of this fold, and that they would all be gathered into one brotherhood of the sons of God. He also said that he had power to lay down his life and power to take it up again. Hearing this, some of the Pharisees left, saying he was mad, but the next day about half of the teachers from Jerusalem confessed that they believed in Jesus.
p165.010: On the Sabbath of January 28, before a crowd of almost three thousand, Jesus taught about trust. He told them to beware of the leaven of the Pharisees, which is hypocrisy, and not to fear those who can kill the body but can do nothing more. Then he asked, “⟦Q 165:3.4⟧Are not five sparrows sold for two pennies?⟦/Q⟧” Not one sparrow is unknown to God, and even the hairs of our heads are numbered, so we should not be afraid of the little things of daily life. You are worth much more than many sparrows.
p165.011: He also told them not to worry about what to say if they were brought before the authorities, because the spirit within them would teach them what to say at that time. Jesus asked how long they would hesitate between two opinions, and he said that the Father never forces anyone to enter the kingdom. The invitation is always open: “⟦Q 165:3.8⟧Whosoever will, let him come and freely partake of the water of life.⟦/Q⟧”
p165.013: A young man asked Jesus to order his brother to divide the inheritance, because his brother would not share it. Jesus said he was not one who divides such things, and he told everyone, “⟦Q 165:4.1⟧Take heed and keep yourselves free from covetousness⟦/Q⟧”. A person's life does not consist in having many possessions. Then he told the story of the foolish rich man. After a good harvest, the rich man said he would build bigger barns and take life easy, eating, drinking, and having fun—but that very night he lost his life, and his wealth passed into other hands. He had stored up treasure on earth but was not rich toward God.
p165.014: When someone asked whether it was a sin to own wealth honestly earned, Jesus said it was not. But it is a sin, he said, if wealth takes over your heart and pulls your heart away from God. “⟦Q 165:4.5⟧where your treasure is there will your heart be also.⟦/Q⟧” Jesus said to let wealth be a servant and not a master, and that a rich man must answer three questions: how much he gathered, how he earned it, and how he used it. Jesus never approved of laziness or of failing to care for one's family, but he taught that material things must always come after the growth of the soul.
p165.015: 5. Talks to the Apostles on Wealth
p165.016: That evening, at Andrew's request, Jesus talked to the apostles again. Since they had left everything and given their lives to the work of the kingdom, he told them not to worry about what they would eat or wear. God feeds the ravens, which neither sow nor reap, and clothes the lilies, which do not toil, more beautifully than Solomon; how much more will he care for you! Worrying will not add a hand's breadth to your height or a single day to your life. If you seek the greater things of heaven, he said, the smaller things of earth will come along with them.
p165.017: But Jesus told them that a great test would soon come, so they must guard against fear and doubt. Like servants waiting for their master to return from a wedding feast, they were to keep their lamps lit and stay awake. For a long while the apostles sat in silence, thinking over this warning.
p165.019: When Peter asked whether this parable was only for the apostles, Jesus answered that trials reveal what is in a person's heart. To the faithful servant who comes through the test, the master entrusts his household. And he said, “⟦Q 165:6.3⟧much has been given to you; therefore will much be required of you.⟦/Q⟧” He also said that the gospel might bring conflict between family members or friends, but that in the hearts of believers there would be great and lasting peace. So he urged them to proclaim this gospel to the whole world.
p165.020: The next day Jesus and the apostles left for the cities of northern Perea to visit the seventy. This paper's teaching—choose trust over worry, and sharing over greed—is a warm comfort for teenagers too, who can easily feel anxious about grades, the future, and what they have.
p166.002: From February 11 to 20, Jesus and the twelve apostles toured the cities and villages of northern Perea. There Abner's associates and the women's corps were preaching the gospel with great success. Jesus reminded the apostles many times that the gospel of the kingdom could spread even without miracles or wonders. From about this time, the gospel came to carry Jesus' teachings more than the person of Jesus himself. But after Jesus' death and resurrection, his followers began to build the early church around miracles and glorious memories of Jesus rather than around these teachings.
p166.004: On the Sabbath of February 18, a wealthy Pharisee of Ragaba named Nathaniel invited Jesus to breakfast as his guest of honor. Jesus sat down at the table without performing the ceremonial washing of hands. Jesus washed his hands to make them clean, but he disliked empty ceremonies. When the Pharisees whispered and sneered, Jesus rebuked them for cleaning the outside of the cup and the platter while filling their hearts with self-righteousness and greed. God, he said, looks not at outward appearance but at the motives of the heart.
p166.005: When a lawyer said that it sounded as if they were being criticized too, Jesus said that the lawyers loaded people with heavy burdens and did not help them, and that they took away the key of knowledge and kept others from entering into the truth. But the door of the kingdom of heaven, he said, is open to all who have faith, and no one can shut it. Hearing this, some of the Pharisees came to believe, but many more made up their minds to find some charge against Jesus.
p166.007: The next day near Amathus, Jesus met ten lepers. Nine were Jews and one was a Samaritan. Normally Jews would have avoided a Samaritan, but their shared suffering had carried them past their prejudice. Simon Zelotes wanted to pass them by because a Samaritan was among them, but Jesus asked, “⟦Q 166:2.3⟧Should we sit in judgment on our fellow men?⟦/Q⟧”
p166.008: Jesus told them to go and show themselves to the priests as the law required, and on the way they were all healed. But only one came back, fell at Jesus' feet, and gave thanks—the Samaritan. Jesus said, “⟦Q 166:2.5⟧your faith has made you whole⟦/Q⟧”, and Simon bowed his head. Jesus taught that the children of the house can easily take blessings for granted, but a stranger cannot help being thankful for a gift received.
p166.010: At Gerasa a Pharisee asked whether few or many would be saved. Jesus answered that there was truth in the old saying that the gate to life is narrow, but that salvation depends above all on each person's choice. Though the gate is narrow, it is wide enough for everyone who sincerely wants to enter, and Jesus himself is that gate.
p166.011: But he warned that there is danger for those who put off entering the kingdom while chasing pleasure and selfishness. Later, when the glory is revealed, it will do no good to try to enter for their own gain. Yet there is no need to be afraid. Everyone who sincerely wants it will find salvation. Jesus said, “⟦Q 166:3.7⟧Behold, I stand at the doors of men's hearts and knock⟦/Q⟧”. In the end, the number of those saved depends on how many answer this invitation.
p166.013: While they were eating lunch on the way to Philadelphia, Thomas asked whether angels or spirit beings could prevent accidents. Jesus asked in return whether they had not seen that he himself did not use heavenly powers for his own life. People of old believed that prosperity was a sign of God's approval and misfortune a sign of God's anger, but Jesus said this was superstition. The Father sends rain on the just and the unjust alike. The eighteen who died when the tower of Siloam fell were not greater sinners than others; they were simply victims of an accident.
p166.014: Jesus said that three kinds of things happen in our lives: ordinary events we share with other people, accidents and misfortunes of nature, and the results of efforts made in wise harmony with natural law. Even the barren fig tree bore rich fruit once it was fertilized and cared for. Health and sickness also come from material causes: “⟦Q 166:4.10⟧health is not the smile of heaven, neither is affliction the frown of God.⟦/Q⟧” The Father gives material things without favoritism, but he gives spiritual gifts according to the faith and will of those who receive them.
p166.016: Of all the cities of Perea, Philadelphia was the one where the most people accepted the gospel. Its synagogue was free from the interference of the Sanhedrin in Jerusalem, so it was always open to Jesus' teaching, and Abner taught there three times a day. This synagogue later became a church and a center for spreading the gospel to the lands of the east.
p166.017: After Jesus left, Abner led the church at Philadelphia, but he disagreed with James and Peter of the Jerusalem church and also with Paul, and he lived somewhat alone. To the end he opposed changing Jesus' teachings to suit other people's tastes. Because of this, the believers at Philadelphia followed the religion that Jesus lived and taught more faithfully than anyone else. Abner remained a faithful teacher of the gospel until he died at the age of eighty-nine. A life that holds on to the truth even when no one notices, and a heart that knows how to be thankful for the grace received, are precious for us too.
p167.002: During the Perean ministry, usually ten apostles traveled with Jesus. That was because at least two apostles always stayed at the Pella camp to teach the people who gathered there. When Jesus arrived at Philadelphia, more than six hundred people were following him. There were no miracles during this period except the healing of the ten lepers, yet the gospel was spreading powerfully. Good news came in from Philadelphia and the nearby villages, and even from Alexandria and Damascus.
p167.004: A wealthy Pharisee of Philadelphia who had accepted Abner's teachings invited Jesus to a Sabbath breakfast as his guest of honor. A member of the Sanhedrin from Jerusalem tried, as he always did, to take the highest seat, and when he was moved to another seat, he was very offended. As the meal was ending, a believer who had long suffered from a disease that made his body swell came in quietly and sat on the floor. Although he had not asked to be healed, Jesus knew the hope and faith in his heart and healed him.
p167.005: Then he taught the guests that when they went to a feast, they should sit not in the place of honor but in the lowest place, because “⟦Q 167:1.5⟧every one who exalts himself shall be humbled, while he who truly humbles himself shall be exalted.⟦/Q⟧” He also told them that when they gave a feast, they should not invite only friends or rich neighbors who could pay them back, but should sometimes invite the poor and the disabled.
p167.007: When a lawyer, trying to break an awkward silence, said, “⟦Q 167:2.1⟧Blessed is he who shall eat bread in the kingdom of God⟦/Q⟧”, Jesus told a parable. A certain ruler prepared a great supper and invited guests, but they all made excuses—they had bought a field, they had bought oxen, they had just married—and did not come. The angry master told his servants to go out into the streets and lanes, the highways and the countryside, and bring in the poor, the outcasts, the blind, and the lame until his house was full.
p167.008: At least one of the Pharisees who had sneered at this story understood its meaning and was baptized that day. The next day the apostles each tried to explain the parable, but Jesus would not explain it for them. He only said, “⟦Q 167:2.4⟧Let every man find out the meaning for himself and in his own soul.⟦/Q⟧”
p167.009: 3. The Woman with the Spirit of Infirmity
p167.010: That Sabbath Jesus taught in the synagogue at Philadelphia. It was the first time since the synagogues had been closed to him by order of the Sanhedrin. After the service Jesus went over to an elderly woman whose body was badly bent and whose face was gloomy. For more than eighteen years she had lived weighed down by fear, and she had lost all the joy of life. When Jesus told her she could be set free “⟦Q 167:3.1⟧if you would only believe⟦/Q⟧”, the woman believed his words and straightened up at once. Her illness had really come not from her body but from her mind.
p167.011: The hostile ruler of the synagogue was angry that someone had been healed on the Sabbath. Jesus asked him in return: if people untie an ox and lead it to water even on the Sabbath, how could it be wrong to set this woman free from her bondage? The congregation rejoiced together, and that ruler of the synagogue eventually lost his position. In this way Jesus set free many people who were bound by fear and depression.
p167.013: One night Martha and Mary of Bethany sent word: “⟦Q 167:4.1⟧Lord, he whom you love is very sick.⟦/Q⟧” Jesus loved their brother Lazarus very much, and he wanted to hurry to him at once. But to give the leaders in Jerusalem one more chance to believe, Jesus decided to show his power over life and death, if the Father would allow it. The Jews of that time believed that the soul left the body completely after the third day of death, so Jesus waited two more days before setting out.
p167.014: The apostles tried to stop him from going into Judea, because the leaders in Jerusalem wanted to kill him. But Jesus said that “⟦Q 167:4.5⟧Lazarus has fallen asleep⟦/Q⟧” and that he was going to wake him, and when the apostles did not understand, he told them plainly that Lazarus was dead. Then Thomas said to his companions, “⟦Q 167:4.7⟧let us go also that we may die with him.⟦/Q⟧” Whenever courage was needed, Thomas was the strong support of the apostles.
p167.016: On the way to Bethany, Jesus taught that salvation is a free gift to all who have faith, and he told the story of the Pharisee and the publican. The Pharisee prayed boasting that he was not like other people, while the publican stood far off and prayed, “⟦Q 167:5.1⟧God be merciful to me a sinner.⟦/Q⟧” It was the publican who went home with God's approval. The Pharisee sought justice; the publican sought mercy.
p167.017: That night at Jericho, the Pharisees tried to trap Jesus with the question of divorce, but Jesus did not let himself be pulled into the argument. Instead he lifted up marriage as the highest of all human relationships, and he rebuked the custom of that day, which let a husband put away his wife for the smallest reason, as unjust to women and children. Jesus supported only teachings that regarded women and men as equal. He also said that marriage is honorable, and that parents who make a home and raise children become partners with those who made heaven and earth.
p167.019: The next morning, the mothers of Jericho crowded around Jesus with their children to have them blessed. When the apostles tried to send them away, Jesus was indignant and said, “⟦Q 167:6.1⟧Suffer little children to come to me; forbid them not⟦/Q⟧”. Then he laid his hands on each child and blessed them. These children hardly knew that they were playing with the Creator of a universe.
p167.020: Jesus taught that beauty is a great help to children when they first learn to worship. Jesus himself loved to talk with the Father among the trees and under the starry sky. A place of worship should be simple and beautiful rather than overly showy, because beauty is most religious when it is most simple and natural.
p167.022: On the way up to Bethany, Nathaniel asked what they should teach about angels. Jesus explained that angels are a separately created order of beings, entirely different from humans. Angels are not people who have died, and people never become angels. Angels do not know everything or have all power, but the loyal angels are pure and holy.
p167.023: Angels are not spies who secretly look into our hearts and report on us, because the Father's spirit already lives within us. Angels help the different parts of the universe keep in touch with one another, and many angels are assigned to serve human beings. When a person begins to seek God, the angels rejoice, and after death they guide the human soul to the new world. Just as the talk was about to go on, Martha came running to meet Jesus. Knowing that unseen help is with us too is a great comfort for anyone who humbly seeks God.
p168.002: When Jesus came over the hill near Bethany, Lazarus had already been dead for four days. That morning the entrance of the tomb had been sealed with a stone. Martha and Mary believed that if Jesus spoke just one word, their brother would get well, so they were very confused when they received the message “⟦Q 168:0.3⟧this sickness is really not to the death.⟦/Q⟧” Lazarus's family was wealthy and respected, and many people had come from Jerusalem and the neighboring villages to comfort them. Among them were some who bitterly hated Jesus.
p168.003: Martha never gave up hope, and she had a neighbor boy watch the road. When she heard that Jesus was coming, she ran out, fell at his feet, and cried, “⟦Q 168:0.6⟧Master, if you had been here, my brother would not have died!⟦/Q⟧” Jesus said, “⟦Q 168:0.7⟧I am the resurrection and the life; he who believes in me, though he dies, yet shall he live.⟦/Q⟧” And Martha confessed that Jesus was the Son of the living God. Then Mary also came running, said the same thing, and wept, and Jesus' soul was moved with compassion. Jesus was deeply stirred, standing between those who truly grieved and enemies who only pretended to grieve.
p168.005: “⟦Q 168:1.1⟧Where have you laid him?⟦/Q⟧” Jesus wept as he followed the sisters to the tomb. The Urantia Book suggests three reasons why Jesus wept: his deep sympathy with the grieving sisters; his distress at the mixture of sincere and pretended mourning; and his knowledge that if he raised Lazarus, Lazarus would suffer severe persecution. The Urantia Book also records that fifteen minutes before Lazarus breathed his last, an order had already been given for his Thought Adjuster (the spirit of God that lives in the human mind) to remain on this world.
p168.006: In front of the tomb, a great host of heavenly beings, unseen by human eyes, had gathered and were waiting under the direction of Gabriel. When Jesus said, “⟦Q 168:1.11⟧Take away the stone⟦/Q⟧”, Martha hesitated, saying that after four days the body would have begun to decay. Jesus told her not to doubt—had he not said that if she only believed, she would see the glory of God? The Jews of that time believed that by the fourth day after death the soul had departed completely, so it became clear that this was truly the raising of a dead man.
p168.008: Jesus looked up to heaven, thanked the Father, and then cried with a loud voice, “⟦Q 168:2.2⟧Lazarus, come forth!⟦/Q⟧” In only twelve seconds Lazarus, wrapped in his grave clothes, began to move and sat up. Jesus told them to unbind him. Apart from the apostles and the two sisters, many people fled home in terror. Lazarus did not know why he was wearing grave clothes, because for those who sleep the sleep of death, no time passes.
p168.009: When Lazarus knelt and gave thanks, Jesus raised him up and said that all who believe this gospel will be resurrected in a more glorious form, and that Lazarus would be a living witness of it. The Urantia Book says that this was the first and the last time on Urantia (our earth) that a dead person was brought back to life in the same body he had before. The news quickly spread all over Jerusalem; many believed, but some closed their hearts even more firmly.
p168.011: The next day the Sanhedrin (the highest Jewish council) met. When a Pharisee proposed putting Jesus to death without a trial, fourteen members objected and walked out, and later five members friendly to Jesus were expelled. The Sanhedrin heard Lazarus's testimony and admitted that he had come back to life, but they blamed it on the power of the devil. They were afraid that all the people would follow Jesus and that there would be a clash with Rome. The high priest Caiaphas said, “⟦Q 168:3.6⟧It is better that one man die, than that the community perish.⟦/Q⟧” Jesus heard this news but was not shaken; he quietly spent the Sabbath and then went back to Pella.
p168.013: On the way to Pella, the apostles asked many questions about answers to prayer, because Lazarus had died even though Jesus had said “⟦Q 168:0.3⟧this sickness is really not to the death⟦/Q⟧”. Jesus explained that prayer is the effort of a finite mind to reach out to the Infinite. Even when a prayer seems unanswered, the answer is often delayed so that a better answer can come. Some prayers are so great that they can be answered only in eternity, and some answers can be recognized only after we have grown spiritually. Sometimes people pray wrong prayers out of ignorance or superstition, and then spirit beings may change those prayers into something right and answer them.
p168.014: Every true prayer is answered in a spiritual way. Just as a child can ask its parents for anything, we have the right to pray freely. And just as parents, in greater wisdom, may delay or change their answer, so does God. Jesus said, “⟦Q 168:4.13⟧Ask and you shall receive⟦/Q⟧”, and he told them that every genuine petition born of the spirit is sure of an answer, but that they must remember the factor of time.
p168.016: Lazarus lived in Bethany until the day Jesus was crucified, and many people were curious about him. But the Sanhedrin decided to kill Lazarus too, since he was a living witness, and he fled across the Jordan to Philadelphia. Soon Martha and Mary sold their land and came there too. Lazarus became the treasurer of the church at Philadelphia and helped Abner, and he died at sixty-seven of the same illness as before. This story shows that even when prayers do not seem to be answered right away, God is answering at a better time and in a better way.
p169.002: On the evening of March 6, Jesus and the ten apostles returned to the Pella camp. It was to be their last week there. Every afternoon Jesus preached to the crowds, and every night he answered the questions of the apostles and disciples. News that Lazarus had been raised had arrived ahead of them, and the camp was buzzing with excitement. Meanwhile, the Pharisees and chief priests were drawing up their charges against Jesus: that he was a friend of publicans and sinners; that he blasphemed by calling God his Father; that he broke the law by healing on the Sabbath; and that he worked miracles by the power of the devil.
p169.004: Speaking about the “⟦Q 169:1.1⟧Grace of Salvation⟦/Q⟧”, Jesus told three stories. The prophets of old had taught people to seek God, but Jesus came to show that while we are seeking God, God is also seeking us. A good shepherd leaves the ninety-nine sheep to search for the one that is lost, and a woman sweeps the whole house again and again until she finds her one lost coin. And even before we repent, the Father has already accepted us. Jesus said that there is great joy in heaven over one sinner who repents, and he agreed that it was right to call him the friend of publicans and sinners.
p169.005: The third story is the parable of the lost son, the prodigal son. A father had two sons. The younger one, cheerful but always avoiding responsibility, took his share of the property, went off to a far country, and wasted it all. When famine came and he was starving while feeding pigs, he came to his senses and decided to go back to his father and ask to be taken in, even as a hired servant. But while the son was still far off, the father ran out and embraced him, and before the son could even finish his apology, the father gave him the best robe and a ring and held a feast: “⟦Q 169:1.10⟧for this my son was dead and is alive again; he was lost and is found.⟦/Q⟧”
p169.006: The older brother, coming back from the field, was angry and would not go into the house. He said that he had worked faithfully for a long time and had never received anything. The father spoke kindly to him too—“⟦Q 169:1.13⟧all this which I have is yours⟦/Q⟧”—and asked him to rejoice with them. The lost sheep shows people who wander off without knowing it; the lost coin shows people who are buried in worldly affairs and spiritually blind; and the prodigal son shows people who leave on their own and then come back—and the Father fully restores them all. Along with the story of the good Samaritan, this parable was one of the stories Jesus loved most to tell.
p169.008: When Simon Zelotes asked what it meant that the people of the world are wiser than the children of the kingdom, Jesus told the story of the shrewd steward. A steward who had wasted his master's money and was about to be dismissed secretly reduced the debts of those who owed his master money, so that he would have friends to welcome him later. Even the master admitted that he had been shrewd in preparing for his future.
p169.009: Jesus did not mean that we should copy dishonesty. He meant that if people work so hard for their own gain, God's workers should work even harder for the kingdom. “⟦Q 169:2.6⟧he who is faithful in little will also be faithful in much⟦/Q⟧”. And no one can serve both God and riches. When the Pharisees, who loved money, sneered and started an argument, Jesus did not argue but withdrew to his tent.
p169.010: 3. The Rich Man and the Beggar
p169.011: When the gathering became noisy, Peter stood up and told an old story that John the Baptist used to tell. There was a rich man who lived in luxury, and a beggar named Lazarus at his gate who longed to eat even the crumbs. After both of them died, Lazarus was comforted in Abraham's bosom while the rich man was in torment. The rich man asked that his brothers be warned, but Abraham answered that those who do not listen to Moses and the prophets would not be persuaded even if someone rose from the dead. Peter explained that this was an old parable, different from the new gospel, and Jesus said nothing about this story.
p169.013: Although Jesus preached the kingdom of God, he never once called God a king. Because the people of his time knew only kings and kingdoms, he used the term 'kingdom of heaven,' but what he meant was a spiritual brotherhood of people, and its head was not a king but the Father in heaven. Jesus called himself the Son of Man and our elder brother. He also did not try to prove by argument that God exists. In fact, Jesus taught only two things about God: that God is spirit, and that he is a Father to all his creatures.
p169.014: What is important is that Jesus never said, “⟦Q 169:4.12⟧Whoso has heard me has heard God⟦/Q⟧”, but he did say, “⟦Q 169:4.12⟧He who has seen me has seen the Father.⟦/Q⟧” God cannot be known merely by understanding words; he can be known only through experience. By looking at Jesus' life, we can see what God is like. Jesus is like a spiritual lens that shows us the invisible God. We cannot fully understand God, but we can know him most surely, just as the apostles knew the Son of Man.
p169.015: Going beyond the idea of a God of the people of Israel alone, Jesus taught that God is the Father of all people and that all people are brothers. The God who rules the universe and the Father who sends his spirit into our minds are the same. Like the father who runs out first to embrace his lost son, God is always waiting for us.
p170.002: On Saturday afternoon, March 11, Jesus preached his last sermon at Pella. Its subject was the 'kingdom of heaven.' The apostles and disciples had often heard the terms “⟦Q 170:0.1⟧kingdom of heaven⟦/Q⟧” and “⟦Q 170:0.1⟧kingdom of God⟦/Q⟧”, but they were confused about what they meant. That was because the hope of a political kingdom to be set up on this earth was too deeply rooted in the minds of the Jews. This paper takes the sermon of that day, adds what Jesus said at other times and what he told the apostles that night, and also explains how the idea of the kingdom changed later in the church.
p170.003: 1. Concepts of the Kingdom of Heaven
p170.004: The old Hebrew scriptures held two ideas of the kingdom: a kingdom that already exists now, and a future kingdom to be completed when the Messiah came. Mixed with these were the later Jewish idea of a worldwide kingdom coming down miraculously from heaven, and the Persian teaching that good would defeat evil at the end of the world. Just before Jesus came, the Jews had combined all of these and were expecting the Messiah to come and begin an age of Jewish triumph.
p170.005: But the kingdom Jesus always taught the apostles was a personal experience—the experience of a person in relationship with the Father in heaven and with neighbors. Jesus' last word was always “⟦Q 170:1.11⟧the kingdom of heaven within you.⟦/Q⟧” The Urantia Book names several reasons why the meaning of this saying became confused for centuries: the idea developed through many stages, the gospel moved from the Jewish land into the gentile world, and the gospel gradually became a religion about Jesus.
p170.007: Jesus' kingdom stands on the truth that God is the Father of all people and that all people are brothers. When people accept this teaching, they are set free from old fears and gain new courage; the poor are comforted; and they come to value spiritual things above material ones. Human life gains a new dignity and noble goals.
p170.008: Jesus tried hard to get people to use “⟦Q 170:2.11⟧the will of God⟦/Q⟧” instead of the term 'kingdom of God.' Instead of a picture of a king and his subjects, he wanted to give them a picture of the Father in heaven and his family, of liberated sons of God gladly serving one another. But he did not succeed. Jesus taught that the kingdom has a stage in this world, in which we do God's will and love our neighbors, and a stage in heaven, where that love is made complete.
p170.009: Two things are needed to enter the kingdom: a childlike faith that opens the heart and trusts the Father, and a heart that hungers for righteousness and truth. Jesus also taught that God has already forgiven our sins, and that when we forgive others, we become able to actually receive that forgiveness.
p170.011: Jesus taught that childlike faith is the key that opens the door of the kingdom, but that once inside, we must grow step by step. The process goes like this: when we forgive others, we experience God's forgiveness; only when we love our neighbor as ourselves can we truly forgive; this love is the highest ethics; and right conduct comes naturally from that love.
p170.012: So true faith always shows itself in a life of serving others. But Jesus did not put good deeds in the place of faith. Faith is the cause, and good deeds are its fruit. Since every act is judged by its motive, the highest goodness is the goodness that comes out naturally, without our even knowing it. The religion of the kingdom is personal, but its fruits spread out to families and to the whole of society.
p170.014: Jesus never defined the kingdom in a single sentence. On this day Jesus described the kingdom in five stages: the inner experience of a person with God; the brotherhood formed by believers; the superhuman kingdom of God, which includes even unseen spirit beings; a new social order in which the will of God is better done; and the age of light and life that will come in the far future. He also stressed, as the heart of the gospel, the worth of the individual, the importance of the will, fellowship with God, the joy of loving service, and the priority of spiritual things over material ones.
p170.015: Jesus promised that he would come again someday, and he also spoke of a future kingdom, but he never said these were the same event. Yet the disciples tied the two together and expected Jesus to return soon and set up a glorious kingdom. The Urantia Book says that the world has never really tried these teachings, but that we should not be discouraged; above all, it urges us never to neglect building the kingdom within our own souls.
p170.017: The Urantia Book also explains how the idea of the kingdom changed after Jesus left. The Jewish believers believed that Jesus would soon return and set up a worldly kingdom, and the gentile believers, following Paul's teaching, came to see Jesus as the redeemer of the church. According to The Urantia Book, the rise of the church itself was natural and helpful, but it was unfortunate that the church almost replaced the spiritual kingdom in the heart that Jesus had spoken of. Becoming a church member is not the same as entering the fellowship of the kingdom, because one is spiritual and the other mainly social.
p170.018: But The Urantia Book speaks of hope. Jesus' teachings have an eternal power, and they will surely bear fruit in the minds of thinking people. The Urantia Book compares today's church to a cocoon in which the kingdom is sleeping, and says that someday it will awaken like a beautiful butterfly. It also says that there may be differences of opinion among believers, but that a lack of spiritual brotherhood cannot be excused. The kingdom of heaven is not a faraway land; it begins now, in our hearts, with the choice to follow God's will.
p171.002: The day after the sermon on the kingdom, Jesus announced that he would go to Jerusalem to keep the Passover. When his followers heard this, they thought that Jesus was at last going to set up the Jewish kingdom in Jerusalem. No matter how often Jesus told them that the kingdom is within, they could not give up their hope of a political kingdom set up by the Messiah.
p171.003: That afternoon Salome, the mother of James and John, came with her two sons and asked that in Jesus' kingdom her sons might sit at his right hand and his left. Jesus asked, “⟦Q 171:0.5⟧Are you able to drink the cup I am about to drink?⟦/Q⟧” and the two answered without thinking that they were able. Jesus said that they would indeed share his suffering, but that those places were not his to give. When the other apostles found out and were angry, Jesus said, “⟦Q 171:0.6⟧the Son of Man came not to be ministered to but to minister⟦/Q⟧”, and whoever wants to be great must first serve others. The two brothers apologized to their companions. In less than a month, on either side of Jesus there would be, not seats of glory, but two criminals on crosses.
p171.005: On March 13, Jesus and the twelve apostles left the Pella camp for the last time and headed for southern Perea. About a thousand disciples went with them. Most of them believed that Jesus would go to Jerusalem and take the throne of David. Two days later, under Andrew's direction, David Zebedee broke up the visitors' camp, where nearly four thousand people had been staying.
p171.006: The Urantia Book also tells what came afterward. David later went to Philadelphia and worked with Abner and Lazarus. After Jerusalem fell, Antioch became the center of Paul's kind of Christianity and spread the gospel westward, while Philadelphia became the center of Abner's version of the kingdom of heaven and sent missionaries to Mesopotamia and Arabia.
p171.008: When they reached the ford of the Jordan and the people began to murmur on learning that Jesus was not going straight to Jerusalem, Jesus climbed onto a large rock and preached the sermon on “⟦Q 171:1.2⟧Counting the Cost.⟦/Q⟧” From now on, he said, anyone who wished to follow him must be ready to give everything to doing the Father's will. Someone who wants to build a tower first sits down and counts the cost, and a king about to go to war first considers whether he can win. In the same way, anyone who wants to be Jesus' disciple must first consider whether he is ready to endure persecution and disappointment.
p171.009: Jesus warned that those who follow him hoping for honor or glory are like salt that has lost its flavor, and he told those who were not willing to drink the cup of suffering with him to go home in peace. After this about five hundred followed Jesus to Heshbon, and the rest went up to Jerusalem. Even so, the apostles still believed that after a short trial, the kingdom they were hoping for would be set up in the end.
p171.011: For more than two weeks Jesus and the apostles toured the villages of southern Perea where the seventy had been working. At Heshbon Jesus met Abner and urged him not to be shaken by whatever happened in Jerusalem, but to go on with his work. This was the last time Abner saw Jesus in the flesh. As he said good-bye, Jesus told Abner that he would pray that he might have the wisdom to love and understand his brethren.
p171.012: The apostles knew that the Sanhedrin had sentenced Jesus to death and ordered that his whereabouts be reported, but this time they were not very afraid. Since they had seen Lazarus raised, they believed that in a crisis Jesus would drive back his enemies with divine power. Many of the apostles could not even imagine that Jesus, “⟦Q 171:3.5⟧the resurrection and the life⟦/Q⟧”, could die.
p171.014: On the night they stayed at Livias, Simon Zelotes and Peter secretly got hold of more than a hundred swords and handed them out. Jesus knew about this but acted as if he did not. Early the next morning Jesus gathered the apostles and told them not to trust in human defenses such as swords. He told them plainly that the Son of Man would be handed over in Jerusalem, mocked, and killed, but that on the third day he would rise. But the apostles could not take these words as they were. In those days 'the third day' was often used to mean 'soon,' so they understood him to mean that after a short struggle the kingdom would rise.
p171.015: Some friendly Pharisees warned Jesus to get away because Herod wanted to kill him. Jesus said that Herod would actually rather have him die in Jerusalem, and he told them to tell “⟦Q 171:4.6⟧that fox⟦/Q⟧” that he would finish his mission in a few days. Then he grieved over Jerusalem: many times he had wanted to gather her children together, “⟦Q 171:4.7⟧even as a hen gathers her own brood under her wings⟦/Q⟧”, but they would not accept him. What gave the apostles the courage to follow him to Jerusalem was the raising of Lazarus, and what held Jesus up in this hard time was the memory of the transfiguration.
p171.017: Near the gate of Jericho there was a beggar named Bartimeus, who had been blind since his youth. He had made up his mind that if Jesus ever came again, he would ask him to open his eyes. When he heard that Jesus was passing by, he cried out, “⟦Q 171:5.2⟧Jesus, Jesus, have mercy upon me!⟦/Q⟧” and when people told him to be quiet, he cried out even louder. Jesus stopped and called him, and Bartimeus threw off his cloak and came running. “⟦Q 171:5.3⟧your faith has made you whole.⟦/Q⟧” At once he received his sight, and he glorified God and told people what had happened.
p171.019: Zaccheus, the chief publican of Jericho, wanted very much to see Jesus, but he was short and could not see over the crowd. So he ran ahead and climbed a sycamore tree by the road. Jesus stopped under it and said, “⟦Q 171:6.1⟧Make haste, Zaccheus, and come down, for tonight I must abide at your house.⟦/Q⟧” Zaccheus was so happy that he almost fell out of the tree.
p171.020: People grumbled that Jesus was staying at the house of a sinner who took the people's money. Then Zaccheus stood up on a chair and declared that he would give half of his goods to the poor, and that whatever he had taken unjustly, he would pay back four times over. Jesus said, “⟦Q 171:6.3⟧Today has salvation come to this home⟦/Q⟧”, and said that the Son of Man had come to seek and to save the lost.
p171.022: Wherever Jesus went, he spread joy. The Urantia Book says that goodness wins respect, but that only when it goes together with graciousness is it loved by people. Because Jesus understood people deeply and loved them sincerely, he could be a true friend. He was never in a hurry, he did not pry into or meddle in other people's affairs, and he was a good listener. People who talked with him felt not as if they were confessing their faults but as if they were talking things over together.
p171.023: Most of the important things Jesus did happened naturally, “⟦Q 171:7.9⟧as he passed by⟦/Q⟧”. Rather than following a plan made in advance, he always kept his heart open to meet the needs of the one person, the one child, he met along the way. Great things happened because not only did people believe in Jesus, but Jesus also deeply believed in people. The Urantia Book says that followers in every age must also learn to do good to others as they pass by, while carrying out their daily duties.
p171.025: On the way up to Bethany, Jesus told the apostles the parable of the pounds. This parable was based on the true story of Archelaus, who tried to become king and was rejected by his people. Jesus told the apostles ahead of time that they were expecting to receive the kingdom in Jerusalem, but that they would be disappointed. A nobleman, leaving for a far country, gave each of his servants one pound. When he returned, one servant had made ten pounds and another five, and they received praise and reward, but the servant who, out of fear, had only wrapped the money in a napkin was rebuked.
p171.026: Later Nathaniel summed up the parable like this: we are not responsible for what is beyond our ability; those who are faithful in small things are faithful in great things; and those who show the same faithfulness, even with fewer opportunities, receive the same reward. After lunch, Jesus pointed west with a bright face and said, “⟦Q 171:8.14⟧Come, my brethren, let us go on into Jerusalem, there to receive that which awaits us⟦/Q⟧”. Being faithful in the small things entrusted to us, without comparing ourselves with others—that is the faithfulness God wants from us.
